discovery: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms and its development into precision quantum sensors
subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / quantum sensing
motivation: Around 1989-1991, Bordé showed that atomic beams undergoing photon-recoil transitions act as matter-wave interferometers. Pritchard's group then demonstrated atom interferometry with nanofabricated gratings, and Kasevich (with Chu) demonstrated light-pulse interferometry with laser-cooled atoms. Together they turned de Broglie's matter waves into practical measuring instruments. Atom interferometers now measure gravity, gravity gradients and rotation with very high precision. They have produced leading determinations of the fine-structure constant and of Newton's G, tests of the equivalence principle at the 10^-12 level, and constraints on dark energy and ultralight dark matter. They are also the basis for proposed detectors of mid-band gravitational waves, such as MAGIS-100 and AION. This work combines deep quantum insight with careful instrument engineering, and it gave fundamental physics a new set of quantum sensors with practical uses as well.
